https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/russ.text: Zelenskyy said Russia launched 35 missiles at Ukraine, including 27 ballistic missiles, and 185 drones. Only one ballistic missile was intercepted, "simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot system", he said. More than a dozen explosions reverberated through the city during several waves of attacks, according to Reuters news agency witnesses. "Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people. And every night without them results in more casualties," Zelenskyy said on the Telegram messaging app. With the war in its fifth year, fighting is raging along roughly 1,200 kilometres of front line. But Russian advances have slowed by more than half this year, and Ukraine has been launching strikes inside Russia, hitting its oil facilities, logistics sites, and weapons production. At the same time, Russia intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine is chronically short of air defences capable of downing ballistic missiles, which travel at several times the speed of sound. Moscow and Kyiv both deny targeting civilians in the war launched by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Saturday's is the second major attack on Kyiv this week after strikes on Thursday killed nine people, including six members of one family in a village near Kryvyi Rih , and a suspected Russian cruise missile landed in Poland. Damage was recorded in seven districts across Kyiv, a city of about 3 million people, the Prosecutor's General Office said after Saturday's attacks. Zelenskyy said that fires broke out across Kyiv and 18 residential buildings, a school, the Lithuanian Embassy, and infrastructure facilities were damaged. The Lithuanian foreign ministry said windows at its embassy had broken, solar collectors were damaged, and the yard was scattered with debris. Ukrainian prosecutors said seven people were killed in the Darnytskyi district on the left bank of the Dnipro river and two more people died in the Solomyanskyi district on the right bank of the city. Dozens of people were injured, including four children who suffered multiple shrapnel wounds and lacerations. The attack comes as Ukraine presses its allies for Patriot air defences. Zelenskyy had met with US President Donald Trump on Wednesday for talks, partly to lobby Washington for licenses to produce Patriots domestically. The Ukrainian leader said following the meeting that Trump had agreed to license the production of the missiles to Kyiv. But the US president appeared to express reservations on Friday, saying that Washington would have to be "very careful" about the decision. On Saturday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said Russia's attacks showed Ukraine needed the weapon urgently. "It is the battle for the skies that will define the trajectory of this war. The stronger the air shield over Ukraine, the closer peace becomes," he said. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has sparked Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II. Tens of thousands have been killed and millions forced to flee their homes due to the fighting, while Moscow now occupies around a fifth of its neighbour — including Crimea, which it annexed in 2014. download our app subscribe to our newsletter

The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » Panoramice » Green Planet » The Green Belt of Bucharest The Green Belt of Bucharest Bucharest, one of Europe's most congested capitals, is taking steps toward sustainable urban development through a Green Belt project banner Terra Verde Daniel Onea , 25.09.2026, 14:00 The initiative aims to create a ring of vegetation around the city to combat pollution and the effects of climate change. Conceived to act as a veritable “oxygen mask” for a city stifled by traffic, the project has an estimated budget of 50 million euros. According to official documents, the first major expropriation and afforestation efforts are expected to begin in 2027, with the vision for full implementation extending to 2050. Beyond merely planting trees, the project aims to create vital ecological corridors and protect wetlands. Ciprian Gălușcă, Executive Director of the Climate Adaptation Platform, highlights the complexity of this undertaking as well as its vital role for the future of the metropolitan area: Ciprian Galusca: “The Green Belt is a project that is as ambitious as it is necessary. We are talking about developing vegetation that plays a key role in mitigating the negative effects of climate change, alongside a comprehensive spatial planning scheme for the Bucharest metropolitan area. We also aim to incorporate features that encourage recreation. We can envision a not-too-distant future where we might spend a full weekend near Bucharest within this Green Belt. During the summer, we could escape the city’s urban heat island effect by relaxing just 30 to 50 kilometers away. To bring this infrastructure to life, however, we first need a plan.” Currently, when we speak of the Green Belt, everyone has a slightly different understanding of the concept. Ciprian Gălușcă, Executive Director of the Climate Adaptation Platform, says that fears regarding a potential economic standstill caused by this ecological ring are completely unfounded. Ciprian Galusca: “For instance, some mayors in the metropolitan area worry that such a project might hinder local development. This is entirely untrue, as examples from Western Europe demonstrate the opposite: creating this type of infrastructure has spurred economic growth and laid the groundwork for a sustainable economy. A brief example: the Green Belt could become a meeting point where local producers and Bucharest residents—who might visit specific areas of the belt—can do their shopping. We could cycle to the forest or to one of the lakes near the city, stopping along the way at a market featuring local products. In other words, the first item on the agenda is to create a vision for this belt. Here, we need input from all relevant stakeholders: local authorities, businesses, Bucharest residents, and the communities living near the infrastructure. We must collectively define our destination and aspirations for the Green Belt, as this is a long-term process that will not be completed in just a year or two. We can look to the example of Vienna, which has been developing the green infrastructure around its capital for over a century. The Green Belt is a living entity; we need a strong, clear, and coherent development vision for it before moving to the implementation phase.” The foundation for this project already exists on the ground, but it requires a unified approach to become a functional network, notes the climate adaptation expert. Ciprian Galusca: “In the first phase, we are starting with the approximately 26,000 hectares of forest in Ilfov County. Currently, these are not managed in the way we would like for a ‘Green Belt’—that is, prioritizing social function, resilience, and climate adaptation. We therefore need to rethink the current forestry management model. Then, there is the network of lakes and pastures which, unfortunately, has lost its connectivity with the forests. Due to extensive real estate development and road infrastructure in the metropolitan area, we will need to find solutions to interconnect these natural zones. The goal is to make them accessible—in a sustainable manner—to local residents and all citizens of the metropolitan area. First and foremost, we must create a pleasant experience for those visiting these places. We have enough natural areas to launch this concept and to develop a vision, an operational plan, and an entity to manage this infrastructure. Subsequently, we can discuss expansion and new afforestation campaigns.” Successful European models demonstrate that environmental protection measures must be accelerated to safeguard the future of major urban centers, emphasizes Ciprian Gălușcă, Executive Director of the Climate Adaptation Platform. Ciprian Galusca: “Protecting the city is a priority. If we want a livable Bucharest in 20 or 30 years—or perhaps even sooner—we must take action. We should have done so already, but now we need to move much faster. For instance, following the deadly heatwaves of the early 2000s, Paris implemented a series of highly ambitious measures. They expanded urban green spaces and established rapid response plans for heatwaves. Today, they are far better prepared than they were 20 years ago. We do not need to reinvent the wheel. Vegetation, forests, and natural areas within and near communities represent the best and most accessible solutions for adapting to climate change.” Thus, the success of the Green Belt depends on close collaboration among all stakeholders and the courage of the authorities to transform existing natural spaces into a coherent network. It is a collective effort, essential not only for air quality but also for the future health of all residents in the Bucharest area. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on October 16, 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on October 16, 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images This Is Europe World news ​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last? As US support ebbs away, looming European elections and growing financial strains across the continent could fracture the precious coalition that has kept Ukraine afloat Jennifer Rankin Brussels correspondent Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.33 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google E urope woke up last Friday to another belligerent outburst from Donald Trump – this time berating Ukraine’s wartime leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy again. Just a few days after his diesel deal with the Kremlin, the US president said Zelenskyy was more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin and blamed Ukraine’s leader for rocketing oil prices – without any reference to the impact of his own war on Iran. The contrast in Europe was obvious. When Zelenskyy walked into the multi-coloured summit room of the European Council headquarters in Brussels that Friday morning, the EU’s 27 leaders burst into applause, getting to their feet to offer big hugs and brisk handshakes. European Council president António Costa told Zelenskyy and the media: “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine ,” calling instead for increased pressure on Russia. Zelenskyy was thankful, pointedly saying he was happy to have “huge support” from “real leaders”. The symbolism was powerful. As US support crumbles, Europe seems to be stepping up. According to the Kiel Institut’s Ukraine Support Tracker , Europe – including non-EU countries such as the UK and Norway – has spent €236bn supporting Ukraine from 2022 to April 2026, compared with a US outlay of €115bn. While Trump is weakening sanctions, Europe is promising more. The EU has passed 21 rounds of sanctions against Russia and last year agreed to raise a €90bn loan for Ukraine – an unprecedented sum for a non-member state. Meanwhile the EU has opened accession negotiations with Kyiv and given shelter to 4.4million Ukrainian refugees. Behind the declarations of Europe’s enduring support, the outlook is more complex and less encouraging for Ukraine, as it approaches its fifth winter since the launch of Russia’s all-out invasion. First, Europe is not able to replace US military dominance in areas such as intelligence. This was brutally exposed by the disruption to the US SpaceX technologies that Ukraine uses in frontline drone operations and air-defences protecting civilians from Russian air attacks. Zelenskyy said the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access, a charge that senior figures in the Trump administration have denied. Ukraine also depends on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles. Deepening the spat, Zelenskyy this week accused the Trump administration of preventing European countries from passing on their Patriot stocks to Ukraine. Secondly, Europe’s monetary support for Ukraine is not evenly spread. Germany is the second-largest donor, having spent €54bn since the start of the war, a particularly crucial contribution since Trump ceased virtually all new US funding. But a report from the Kiel Institut describes this funding as “sizeable but not exceptional” given the scale of the German economy. Four Nordic countries together have given more than Germany, even though they total only a third of Germany’s population, the researchers note. The EU’s other big economies, France and Italy, give less than Germany. The Nordic, Baltic and other north European states are Ukraine’s most generous donors when contributions are measured against national income, according to the Kiel Institut. Denmark, for instance, spends an equivalent to 4.17% of its gross domestic product supporting Ukraine, and Estonia 3.77%, compared with 1.49% spent by Germany, 1.1% by France, 1% by Italy and 0.86% by the UK. With Ukraine’s huge bill to defend itself growing, and Russia’s relentless attacks continuing to wreak a heavy toll, these more generous donors might arguably feel Europe’s biggest economies – and other western allies – could do more to shoulder these ever-rising costs. Top donors to Ukraine by percentage of GDP View image in fullscreen Financial aid from 24 January 2022 to 31 August 2026 as a % of a country’s 2021 GDP. Illustration: Guardian graphic/Source: Kiel Institute for the World Economy Thirdly, and most critically, Europe’s support for Ukraine could be reaching its limits, as Europe enters a supercycle of elections in which the far-right are expected to make gains. National votes are due in Spain, France, Poland and Italy, four of the five biggest EU member states by population. Mujtaba Rahman , managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group, argued that the biggest risk for Ukraine is not Trump’s opinions, but the potential for European support to fragment. There is a risk 2027 will be the year “when political reality, electoral reality, policy reality, economic reality catches up with Europe and prevents it being able to go further in its support for Ukraine”, he said. France’s elections could be the most consequential. The far-right leader and frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seeking to present herself as the candidate to restore order and security, after days of rioting and looting across French cities. She has also vowed to cease aid to Ukraine within six months of taking office “because we simply cannot do it any more”. Speaking to the Financial Times (£) , Le Pen vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget, which raises questions about a proposed €100bn fund for Ukraine in the upcoming 2028-34 budget cycle. Beyond Ukraine, her election could plunge the EU into a deep internal crisis that will consume political energies and attention. Putin’s ‘strategic patience’ rewarded? skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen US patience is running out with Ukraine as US special envoy Steve Witkoff meets with Vladimir Putin in Russia. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Reuters “European support for Ukraine is already fragmenting,” argued Rahman, who points out the €90bn loan for Ukraine was agreed by only 24 EU countries (Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out). But a Le Pen victory could tilt the balance, especially if anti-Ukraine parties make gains in Spain, Poland and Italy. “Le Pen is the biggest gamechanger because she will provide cover for many other countries to say: ‘enough is enough, we can’t keep funding,’” Rahman said. That scenario paints “a really dark picture for Ukraine, a really sad picture for Ukraine” he said. “Because it’s not about Ukraine’s performance on the battlefield – Ukraine has done a remarkable job of holding the line. This is the risk Europe has been talking about for a very long time, and has promised Ukraine many times it would not allow to happen: that through strategic patience, Russia gains in the negotiating room what it has not been able to gain on the battlefield. And that is precisely the risk Ukraine is now confronting.” To head off this risk, EU leaders will seek to shore up support for Ukraine by agreeing another funding plan. The head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, confirmed that Kyiv has a €70bn funding gap in 2027, although she expects Ukraine’s other international partners to help raise the sum. Jana Kobzová, co-director of the European Security Programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said an EU leaders summit in December will be the moment when “we should have a clear idea and mechanism” on providing the €70bn for Ukraine ahead of key elections. “I think the urgency and the consciousness on the side of the European leaders is already there.” To some extent, EU Russia policy is protected, after a recent decision to keep sanctions in place for three years, avoiding the need for divisive rollover decisions every six months. But a Le Pen victory in six months’ time could lead to a bigger problem than financing Ukraine, suggests Kobzová. “If there is a huge shift in Europe as a result of these elections that are going to affect the way the EU itself works, then Ukraine might become collateral damage.” Guardian live Q&A View image in fullscreen Alexander Hurst and Rokhaya Diallo. Belgium: Prince Harry and Meghan visit EU Parliament for child safety event Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 10 November 2026 - 16:37 GMT+1 Prince Harry and his wife Meghan visited the European Parliament in Brussels, on Tuesday 10 November, to discuss the dangers children face online. The couple met families affected by online abuse before Harry addressed the gathering. … More The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were photographed alongside European Parliament President Roberta Metsola after arriving at the institution. The couple also spent around ten minutes meeting families whose children had been affected by online abuse , before Harry took to the podium to address the gathering. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Footage shows the couple arriving together, posing for photographs with Metsola and Harry delivering his speech . The visit forms part of their public engagement with online child protection , an issue on which they have repeatedly sought to raise awareness. The appearance comes just days after Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was charged over the alleged possession of child sexual abuse images. It marks the Duchess of Sussex's first public appearance since his arrest , bringing additional attention to an event focused on protecting children from online harm. The Brussels event focused on the risks children face on digital platforms and the experiences of families affected by online abuse. By meeting those families and addressing the issue at the European Parliament, Harry and Meghan drew attention to the importance of child safety in an increasingly digital world.
